query: For a damaged high-value component made from a material whose physical and microstructural characteristics make traditional fusion-welding repair ineffective because of hot-cracking risk, what intervention could enable continued service without replacing the entire part under aggressive operating conditions? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to traditional fusion-welding repair, the relevant operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a laser‐cladded high‐entropy alloy (HEA) overlay repair will restore serviceability of a damaged component by avoiding the hot‐cracking issues typical of fusion welding, thereby enhancing crack resistance and high‐temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐value component made from a high‐entropy alloy with a microstructure susceptible to hot cracking during fusion welding repair.
generation.intervention: Laser cladding repair using a tailored HEA coating (for example, a composition similar to FeCrNiTiZr or another design that minimizes low‐melting phases) deposited onto the damaged area with low dilution and rapid solidification.
generation.conditions: Aggressive high-temperature operating conditions and cyclic mechanical loading; laboratory tests should mimic service environments such as 800–1200 °C with thermal cycling and bending/ fatigue loads.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, fine-grained overlay microstructure with minimized low-melting or segregated phases at the interface, which reduces residual stresses and inhibits crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: The laser cladding process delivers a localized, low heat input deposition that rapidly solidifies the HEA overlay. This limits the formation of liquation or intergranular films that usually promote hot cracking in fusion-welded repairs. The overlay’s refined microstructure and strong metallurgical bond to the substrate reduce thermal gradients and stress concentrations, thereby mitigating crack initiation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to traditional fusion welding repair, the laser-clad repaired region will exhibit fewer or no hot-cracks and maintain superior mechanical and fatigue performance under high-temperature service, extending the component's life without full replacement.
generation.baseline: Traditional fusion-welding repair of similar damage, which is ineffective due to the high risk of hot-cracking and resulting premature failure under aggressive conditions.
generation.boundary: The overlay’s benefits are expected to hold under service temperatures ranging approximately from 800 °C to 1200 °C and under cyclic thermal and mechanical load conditions. Effectiveness may be limited if the substrate or environment induces excessive interfacial stresses or corrosion that compromises bond integrity.
generation.uncertainty: While laser cladding shows promise in forming crack-resistant overlays, the exact magnitude of performance improvement and long-term interfacial stability under extended cyclic loading require further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical high-entropy alloy component specimens with controlled simulated damage. Repair half of the specimens using the proposed laser cladding HEA overlay and the other half using traditional fusion welding methods. Subject both groups to accelerated thermal cycling (e.g., 800–1200 °C) and mechanical fatigue or three-point bending tests while monitoring microstructural integrity and crack development through optical/ electron microscopy and mechanical property measurements.
measurements: Frequency and size distribution of hot cracks (via microscopy)
Microstructural analysis (grain size, presence of liquation phases)
Bond integrity at the repair interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-clad repaired specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in hot-cracking incidence, or if their mechanical performance (fatigue life, bending strength) is inferior or not improved relative to the fusion-welded specimens under the simulated aggressive conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Statistical evidence suggests that 70% of mold failures are attributable to wear, which not only causes a waste of resources but also escalates the costs of remanufacturing. However, since wear failures typically initiate at the surface, enhancing the mechanical properties of the mold surface has become a focal point of research [,]. Nowadays, the surface modification technologies mainly include thermal spraying [], anodic oxidation [], physical vapor deposition (PVD) [,], chemical vapor deposition (CVD) [], and laser cladding [,,,,,,,,]. Among them, laser cladding offers significant benefits including low dilution rates, rapid cooling, and robust metallurgical bonding [,]. Consequently, it is an effective method for repairing damaged areas and enhancing the surface wear resistance of H13 steel. Existing research about the elevated temperature friction and wear performance of coatings is lacking, particularly in comparative analyses of wear resistance between coatings and H13 steel at varying experimental temperatures. Consequently, a new FeCrNiTiZr high-entropy alloy which has high hardness and good elevated temperature wear resistance was designed by referring to the classical FeCoCrNiAl high-entropy alloy system and fabricated on H13 steel. Its microstructural evolution and hardness were systematically studied; the elevated temperature wear mechanisms at varying experimental temperatures were especially investigated. The results show that this coating can be used as an excellent repair material for H13 hot-working tool steel.

In the context of the rapid advancement of the modern manufacturing industry, optimizing the surface properties of materials has become increasingly critical for enhancing product performance, prolonging service life, and improving production efficiency []. As an advanced surface engineering technique, laser cladding has demonstrated significant potential in fabricating functional coatings with tailored properties on substrate surfaces. This technology has found extensive applications in various industrial sectors, particularly in mold manufacturing and mechanical engineering fields, owing to its unique advantages in surface modification and repair []. H13 hot-work die steel, a medium-carbon chromium-molybdenum alloy steel, is widely employed in hot-stamping and die-casting applications due to its excellent combination of toughness, thermal fatigue resistance, and wear resistance at elevated temperatures []. However, under severe service conditions, H13 steel encounters significant operational challenges [].
